metadata.title: Identifying Key Contextual Factors of Digital Reading Literacy Through a Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS digital reading data for Grade 4 students from 14 countries and economies (74,692 students; 2,875 schools). The manuscript describes merging student, parent, teacher, and principal questionnaires and then applying k-nearest neighbor (kNN) imputation and standardization before training/testing the SVM classifier. No complex survey weighting or replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, and the ML pipeline is described as a standard random 80/20 split with five-fold cross-validation. Because SVM with RFE is not natively weight-aware in the way ILSA scaling/estimation is, the analysis appears to proceed without applying PIRLS sampling weights, which may limit population-representativeness and uncertainty quantification under the clustered sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS digital reading data for Grade 4 students from the 14 participating countries and economies (Sweden, Chinese Taipei, United States, United Arab Emirates, Canada, Denmark, Georgia, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Norway, Portugal, Singapore, Slovenia). The target was constructed by dichotomizing international digital reading benchmarks: students at advanced/high levels were labeled as high-performing digital readers, and students at intermediate/low levels were labeled as non–high-performing digital readers. The analytic dataset was further processed by imputing missing values for contextual features using kNN and standardizing features (mean 0, SD 1) prior to SVM training; no additional grade/school-type restrictions are described.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS Grade 4 Digital Reading (14 countries/economies)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SVM with recursive feature elimination (RFE) — Top 20 features: five-fold CV average AUC=90.01%, sensitivity=80.65%, specificity=83.51%; test set AUC=90.30%, accuracy=82.54%, sensitivity=80.73%, specificity=83.98%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS Grade 4 Digital Reading the study leveraged print reading levels, reading self-efficacy, home resources for learning, talk about reading in class, and books in the home to predict digital reading level (high vs non–high-performing), finding that these contextual factors—especially reading self-efficacy and home resources—discriminated high-performing digital readers with high discrimination (test AUC=90.30%). This indicates that strengthening home literacy resources and self-efficacy supports, alongside classroom discussion practices, may be effective levers for improving early digital reading performance, though the cross-sectional design and lack of causal identification mean causality cannot be inferred.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed PIRLS 2016 ePIRLS digital reading for Grade 4 students from 14 countries/economies (N=74,692) and constructed a dichotomous target using PIRLS international digital reading benchmarks (advanced/high vs intermediate/low). Using an SVM classifier with recursive feature elimination and a fixed top-20 feature set, the model achieved strong discrimination: five-fold cross-validation average AUC=90.01% (sensitivity=80.65%, specificity=83.51%) and test-set AUC=90.30% with accuracy=82.54% (sensitivity=80.73%, specificity=83.98%). The most influential predictors included print reading levels, reading self-efficacy, home resources for learning, teacher prompts for students to talk about what they read, and books in the home. Missing contextual-feature values were imputed via kNN and features were standardized; however, the paper does not report the use of PIRLS sampling/replicate weights, and the cross-sectional nature limits causal interpretation.
